title: Articles of Confederation
notes: Cited for: The Articles of Confederation were adopted by Congress in November 1777 but not fully ratified by the states until March 1, 1781. Under the Articles, Congress could request money and troops from the states but had no power to make them pay.

title: Articles of Confederation, 1777–1781
publisher: Office of the Historian, US Department of State
notes: Cited for: The weak national response to Shays’ Rebellion convinced many leaders that a stronger central government was needed, feeding the movement for the Constitutional Convention.

title: Articles of Confederation: March 1, 1781
publisher: The Avalon Project, Yale Law School
notes: Cited for: Under the Articles of Confederation, each state had one vote in Congress. Any change to the Articles had to be agreed in Congress and then confirmed by the legislatures of every state.

title: Shays's Rebellion
notes: Cited for: In 1786, armed bands in Massachusetts protesting high taxes and hard times forced courts to close to stop foreclosures and debt cases. In January 1787, Daniel Shays led an attack on the federal arsenal at Springfield; it was driven back, and militia routed the rebels at Petersham in February.

title: Shays' Rebellion
notes: Cited for: Most of the rebels were farmers in western Massachusetts, many of them Revolutionary War veterans, hit hard by new state taxes.

title: Constitutional Convention
notes: Cited for: The Constitutional Convention met at the Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia from May 25 to September 17, 1787; 55 delegates took part, and Rhode Island sent none. George Washington was elected to preside over the Constitutional Convention. The Virginia Plan, offered by Edmund Randolph, proposed a two-house legislature with each state represented according to its population or...

title: A Great Compromise
notes: Cited for: The Great Compromise, named for Connecticut delegates Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth, gave the House seats by population and the Senate equal seats for every state. The Constitutional Convention adopted the Great Compromise on July 16, 1787, by a margin of one vote.

title: Three-fifths compromise
notes: Cited for: The Constitution counted three-fifths of the enslaved population when dividing House seats and direct taxes among the states. Neither the word slave nor the word slavery appears in the original, unamended Constitution.

title: A Covenant with Death and an Agreement with Hell
notes: Cited for: On July 4, 1854, at an abolitionist rally in Framingham, Massachusetts, William Lloyd Garrison burned a copy of the Constitution. Garrison called the Constitution “a covenant with death, and an agreement with hell.”

title: Frederick Douglass
notes: Cited for: Frederick Douglass once shared Garrison’s view, but in 1851 he broke with him, arguing that the Constitution was a valid legal document that could be used for emancipation.

title: Frederick Douglass, The Constitution: Is it Pro-Slavery or Anti-Slavery? (1860)
notes: Cited for: Douglass argued that the Constitution’s own words, which never named slavery, should be read in favor of liberty, not the framers’ hopes.

title: Full Text of The Federalist Papers
notes: Cited for: The Federalist, 85 essays by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay, appeared in New York newspapers from October 1787 to May 1788 to urge New Yorkers to ratify the Constitution.

title: Anti-Federalists
notes: Cited for: Anti-Federalists, including Patrick Henry, feared a single national government, upper-class dominance, weak separation of powers and the loss of local control. The Anti-Federalists lost the ratification fight, but their agitation led to the addition of the Bill of Rights.

title: The Bill of Rights: How Did it Happen?
notes: Cited for: George Mason, a delegate to the Constitutional Convention, refused to sign the Constitution because it lacked a bill of rights. Federalists first argued that a bill of rights was unnecessary because the new government could use only the powers the Constitution listed. With ratification in danger in Massachusetts, Federalists agreed that the First Congress would consider amendments...

title: George Washington
notes: Cited for: George Washington is the only president elected unanimously by the Electoral College, in both 1789 and 1792.

title: George Washington
notes: Cited for: Among the precedents Washington set was creating the president’s cabinet. Washington retired after two terms, a precedent every president followed until Franklin D. Roosevelt.

title: “His Highness, The President” and the First Congress: Moving Toward Republicanism
notes: Cited for: The Senate proposed calling the president “His Highness the President of the United States of America and Protector of their Liberties,” but the House rejected any title and the Senate gave way.

title: Ona Judge Escapes to Freedom
notes: Cited for: On May 21, 1796, Ona Judge, an enslaved maid, escaped from the President’s House in Philadelphia while George and Martha Washington ate dinner. Ona Judge had learned that Martha Washington planned to give her to a granddaughter. Washington tried to have Ona Judge recaptured, but she lived the rest of her life in New Hampshire, legally still a fugitive, until her death in 1848.

title: The First Bank of the United States
notes: Cited for: Alexander Hamilton, the first secretary of the Treasury, urged Congress to create a national bank. Jefferson argued that the Constitution did not give Congress power to create corporations, including a national bank. Jefferson pictured a mainly agrarian country and feared the bank would favor financiers and merchants over plantation owners and family farmers. Washington signed the...

title: Debate on a National Bank, 1790–1791
publisher: Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History
notes: Cited for: After Congress passed a bank bill in February 1791, Washington asked his cabinet, including Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson and Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton, whether it was constitutional. Jefferson warned that going beyond the powers the Constitution gave Congress would be “to take possession of a boundless field of power.” Hamilton answered that implied powers were...

title: Democratic-Republican Party
notes: Cited for: Jefferson’s supporters, favoring states’ rights and a strict reading of the Constitution, organized in 1792 as the Republican Party, later called the Democratic-Republicans. Hamilton’s Federalists favored a strong central government and a loose reading of the Constitution. The Republicans charged that the Federalists had aristocratic attitudes and that their policies favored the...

title: United States presidential election of 1800
notes: Cited for: In the election of 1800, the Democratic-Republican Thomas Jefferson defeated the Federalist president, John Adams. Because electors cast two votes without marking which was for president, Jefferson and his running mate Aaron Burr each received 73 electoral votes. The House of Representatives broke the tie on February 17, 1801, electing Jefferson on the 36th ballot. Alexander...

title: The Election of 1800
notes: Cited for: The 12th Amendment, ratified in 1804, gave president and vice president separate electoral votes.

title: First Inaugural Address of Thomas Jefferson
publisher: The Avalon Project, Yale Law School
notes: Cited for: In his inaugural address of March 4, 1801, Jefferson said: “We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.”

title: Louisiana Purchase, 1803
publisher: Office of the Historian, US Department of State
notes: Cited for: In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana territory, about 828,000 square miles between the Mississippi River and the Rocky Mountains, from France for $15 million. Jefferson, who favored a strict reading of the Constitution, doubted that it allowed him to buy territory.

title: Louisiana Purchase
notes: Cited for: The Louisiana Purchase doubled the size of the United States. The purchase gave the United States France’s imperial claim to land still largely occupied by Native peoples: the sole right to obtain it from them by treaty or conquest.

title: Sacagawea
notes: Cited for: Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led the Corps of Discovery, an expedition that traveled from 1804 to 1806. Sacagawea, her husband Toussaint Charbonneau and her son Jean Baptiste, born in February 1805, left the Mandan and Hidatsa villages with the Corps that spring. Sacagawea was not mainly a guide: she translated with the Shoshone, and her presence signaled the expedition’s...

title: Sacagawea
notes: Cited for: Sacagawea was a Lemhi Shoshone woman captured about 1800 by a Hidatsa raiding party and taken to their villages on the Knife River. In August 1805 the expedition met a Shoshone band led by Sacagawea’s brother, Cameahwait, and the reunion helped Lewis and Clark obtain horses to cross the mountains.

title: War of 1812
notes: Cited for: President James Madison signed the declaration of war against Britain on June 18, 1812.

title: The War of 1812, 1812–1815
publisher: Office of the Historian, US Department of State
notes: Cited for: Americans went to war over the Royal Navy’s impressment of American sailors, British trade restrictions and British support for Native resistance on the frontier. The Treaty of Ghent, signed on Christmas Eve 1814, restored the prewar boundaries.

title: Tecumseh
notes: Cited for: Tecumseh’s younger brother Tenskwatawa, the Prophet, gave the movement spiritual backing, and in 1808 the brothers founded Prophetstown on the Wabash and Tippecanoe rivers. In the War of 1812, Tecumseh allied with the British, and General Isaac Brock placed him in command of all Native forces.

title: Indigenous Peoples: War of 1812
notes: Cited for: The War of 1812 ended without a clear winner, but Indigenous peoples were its real victims, their lands and futures drastically altered. The Shawnee leader Tecumseh urged Native nations from Canada to the Gulf of Mexico to set aside rivalries and unite to protect their cultures and lands. Tecumseh was killed at the Battle of the Thames on October 5, 1813, and his dream of a unified...

title: Tippecanoe
notes: Cited for: In November 1811, William Henry Harrison’s force fought the Battle of Tippecanoe and destroyed Prophetstown.
